item.research_question: How does the elemental stability inherent in High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) due to high configurational entropy and/or sluggish diffusion affect elemental dissolution in molten fluoride salts, specifically regarding the corrosion performance and thermal stability of Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5?
item.material_system: Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 High Entropy Alloy (FCC structure) and 316 H stainless steel (reference)
item.processing_route: Arc melting (Arcast Arc 200) followed by high-temperature homogenization at 1200 °C in a vacuum environment for 48 hours in quartz tubes with a titanium getter; samples exposed to molten FLiBe (2LiF-BeF2) at 700 °C for 1000 hours
item.test_conditions: Molten FLiBe salt at 700 °C for 1000 hours; salt purified by hydro-fluorination with H2/HF sparging; samples suspended in 316 L stainless steel capsules
key_findings: The HEA experienced a mass loss of approximately 3.4 mg/cm2, significantly higher than the 0.26 mg/cm2 loss in 316 H stainless steel.
Mn concentration in the salt increased from 4 to 349 ppm after exposure to the HEA, indicating rapid Mn dissolution.
Cr concentration in the salt remained nearly unchanged (6 to 263 ppm in 316 H, negligible change in HEA), showing Cr retention in the HEA.
Mn depletion in the near-surface region of the HEA extended to a depth of approximately 40 µm.
A new BCC phase with nominal composition Cr67Fe13Mn18.5Ni1.5 precipitated, confirmed by bulk XRD and CALPHAD predictions.
The BCC phase fraction was predicted to be approximately 4% at 700 °C in the original alloy.
Needle-shaped Cr-rich particles were observed precipitating beneath the surface, with concentration varying with distance from the surface.
item.mechanism: Mn acts as a sacrificial element due to its lower standard Gibbs free energy of formation for MnF2 compared to CrF2 and its higher diffusion coefficient; the dissolution of Mn creates a Mn/MnF2 redox buffer in the salt that fixes the potential at a level where Cr dissolution is thermodynamically unfavorable, while the loss of Mn from the alloy matrix drives the precipitation of a Cr-rich BCC phase.
item.limitations: The study does not determine how much Mn in the salt is required to reach a satisfactory buffer level; it is not sufficient to draw conclusions about the role of high entropy of mixing and sluggish diffusion in corrosion behavior based on this single alloy; phase separation was not observed in previous studies because they were performed at lower temperatures or shorter times.
item.future_work: Further experimental results with various HEAs in different salt media are needed to better understand HEA behavior; the amount of Mn required to reach a satisfactory buffer level should be studied; long-term aging experiments are needed to assess HEA phase stability.
quotes: Results show that the HEA lost a higher mass compared to the reference 316 H stainless steel due to the dissolution of Mn into the molten salt.
The loss of Mn from the alloy appeared to discourage the dissolution of Cr in the molten fluoride salts which is widely recognized as the mechanism of corrosion degradation.
Thermal exposure at 700 °C for 1000 hours also led to the precipitation of an additional BCC phase Cr67Fe13Mn18.5Ni1.5, which was confirmed by CALPHAD predictions.
